question.text: Per NISM Ch 1.4.1, which statement about the real risk-free rate is CORRECT?

answer.text: The real risk-free rate equals the 10-year G-sec yield plus the repo rate.
The real risk-free rate is always higher than the nominal risk-free rate in inflationary environments.
The real risk-free rate is a SEBI-published monthly number used for AIF hurdle-rate calibration.
The real risk-free rate is the basic rate of return assuming no inflation and no uncertainty about future cashflows; it is the compensation paid for postponing consumption.

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Per Chapter 1.4.1, 'Real risk free rate is the basic rate of return or interest rate, assuming no inflation and no uncertainty about future cashflows. It is the compensation paid for postponing the consumption.' It is determined by subjective factors (desire for consumption) and objective factors (investment opportunities, real growth). **The Trap:** Option A invents a formula. Option C is the opposite of truth — in inflationary environments, nominal > real. Option D invents a SEBI publication. **Cross-Exam Context:** X-A/X-B (IA L1/L2) and XV (RA) test the real-rate concept in financial-planning and cost-of-capital questions. XXI-B (PM) tests it for portfolio optimisation. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** When you benchmark your private-credit AIF against a 'risk-free rate', state explicitly whether you are using nominal or real. LPs in a 6% inflation regime read a 10% gross IRR very differently from a 4% real IRR. Clarity here prevents post-hoc carry disputes.
